name: The Epic of Gilgamesh: A New Translation, Analogues, Criticism (Norton Critical Edition), translated and edited by Benjamin R. Foster
date: 2001 (W. W. Norton, first edition, paperback ISBN 9780393975161; some listings give June 2001, Norton's own description gives December 2001). Second, revised and expanded Norton Critical Edition 2019 (ISBN 9780393643985). Foster's translation also appears in the Norton Anthology of World Literature
creator: Benjamin R. Foster (Laffan Professor of Assyriology and Babylonian Literature, Yale; curator of the Yale Babylonian Collection), who translated the Akkadian epic. Douglas Frayne translated the Sumerian Gilgamesh poems and Gary Beckman the Hittite version. Published by W. W. Norton
form: Verse translation inside a critical edition: the Akkadian epic in lineated English verse, followed by 'Analogues' (seven Sumerian Gilgamesh poems, the Hittite Gilgamesh, related sources including a Babylonian parody of the epic) and 'Criticism' (essays by Thorkild Jacobsen, William L. Moran, Rivkah Harris and others, plus a poem by Hillary Major), with introduction, glossary, illustrations of Near Eastern artefacts and bibliography
translator_access: Direct. Foster is a professional Assyriologist who reads Akkadian and translates from the cuneiform editions line by line. In a 2016 interview he said: 'I just do it, line by line, comparing various other versions in other languages to see what they do,' and that he tries 'to use the same English word for the same Babylonian word each time if I can, but I'm not slavish about that' (World Literature Today, Jan 2017). The Sumerian and Hittite analogues are the work of specialist colleagues (Frayne, Beckman), not a crib
scholarly_adviser: N/A in the poet-plus-crib sense: Foster is himself the specialist. The edition is a team effort, with Douglas Frayne (Sumerian) and Gary Beckman (Hittite) as co-translators of the analogues
versions_used: Standard Babylonian eleven-tablet epic as the spine, harmonised with Old Babylonian and other Akkadian manuscripts where the Standard text is broken (e.g. Siduri's 'let your stomach be full' speech comes from the Old Babylonian Sippar tablet). Foster calls this 'Gilgamesch-Harmonie': 'My rendering sews together material often centuries apart in time.' Sumerian poems (including Bilgames and the Netherworld) and the Hittite version are given separately as analogues. The 2001 edition predates George's 2003 critical edition and the Sulaymaniyah tablet (published 2014); the 2019 edition revises the translation using George (2003), Maul (2005), new manuscripts and philological work [uncertain: whether the 2019 text incorporates the Sulaymaniyah Tablet V lines]
non_standard_material: Largely merged into a single running narrative for readability, which Foster justifies by audience: 'my intended audience was a college literature class.' Old Babylonian passages are inserted where the Standard version fails, with the source flagged in headings or footnotes rather than by a distinct typeface throughout [uncertain: exact marking convention in the print edition]. Material from other languages is kept out of the main text and set in the separate Analogues section
gap_policy: Shown, but not fussily. Foster marks significant breaks and leaves them open rather than inventing text, but restorations are silently integrated: 'I mark significant breaks, where several words are lost, but generally do not use a convention, such as a question mark or italics, to show whether or not the restoration is certain or only a guess.' He argues that 'relentlessly marking minor problems with the manuscripts is largely a useless exercise in the typesetter's craft.' Harmonising with Old Babylonian material bridges several of the largest lacunae
typography_of_absence: Moderate. Ellipses and brackets mark the larger breaks (one account describes the text as 'pockmarked with ellipses and brackets'), but there are no '(?)' markers or italic restorations of the Kovacs or George type, so the page reads as a poem with visible holes rather than a transcript of damage. Explanatory footnotes sit at the foot of the page [uncertain: frequency of brackets vs ellipses]
tablet_xii: Dropped from the epic. Foster treats Tablet XII as a partial Akkadian translation of a Sumerian poem appended later because it seemed germane, and omits it in favour of the fuller Sumerian original (Bilgames and the Netherworld) translated by Douglas Frayne in the Analogues. The epic therefore ends at Tablet XI with the walls of Uruk, closing the ring begun in the prologue
turning_point: Enkidu's death (Tablets VII-VIII) is the hinge, since Foster frames the epic as about 'the two most important human concerns, love and death' and his interview stresses the Babylonian poet's genius in promoting Enkidu from servant (as in the Sumerian poems) to friend. Because Foster harmonises in the Old Babylonian Siduri speech, Tablet X carries an explicit philosophical counter-offer ('The eternal life you are seeking you shall not find'), which Gilgamesh rejects. The practical lesson arrives with the snake in Tablet XI ('I have done a good deed for a reptile!'), and the closing walls of Uruk turn loss into acceptance
arc_interpretation: Grief leading to acceptance of mortality, framed by kingship and friendship. Foster reads the hero as someone a reader can see as 'both grand and imperfect, different from other people but ultimately the same', and names love and death as the poem's subjects (World Literature Today interview). Evidence in the text: Siduri's carpe diem speech is present, so the reader sees the answer Gilgamesh refuses; his outburst after the snake ('For whom, Ur-Shanabi, have my arms been toiling? / For whom has my heart's blood been poured out?') marks the collapse of the quest; and the final return to the walls of Uruk offers the city and the written record as the only durable achievements. The critical essays (Jacobsen's reading of the epic as a story of maturation, Moran on the epic's shape) push the maturity reading further for students [uncertain: exact essay titles in 2001 edition]
key_passages: Shamhat and Enkidu (Tablet I): Foster renders it compactly, 'Shamhat loosened her garments, she exposed her loins, he took her charms ... Six days, seven nights was Enkidu aroused, flowing into Shamhat' [uncertain: attribution of this wording to Foster]. Siduri's advice (Tablet X, Old Babylonian material merged in): 'Gilgamesh, wherefore do you wander? / The eternal life you are seeking you shall not find ... As for you, Gilgamesh, let your stomach be full, / Always be happy, night and day. / Make every day a delight.' Death in the bedchamber (Tablet XI): Gilgamesh despairs that death lurks in his bedroom and wherever he turns [uncertain: Foster's exact wording not verified]. After the snake: 'For whom, Ur-Shanabi, have my arms been toiling? / For whom has my heart's blood been poured out? / For myself I have obtained no benefit, / I have done a good deed for a reptile!' Closing walls of Uruk: 'Go up, Ur-Shanabi, pace out the walls of Uruk. / Study the foundation terrace and examine the brickwork', repeating the prologue's questions about kiln-fired brick and the seven masters who laid the foundations
diction_and_metre: Free lineated verse, one English line per Akkadian line where possible, with the couplet parallelism of the original kept visible. Modern, plain, readable American English with occasional elevated or slightly formal turns ('wherefore do you wander'). Foster tested lines by ear: 'I also felt it was very important to read aloud what I had done. That way the lame lines came through with discouraging clarity.' A reviewer praises it for retaining 'the poetic rhythm of the Akkadian original'
sample_line: "The eternal life you are seeking you shall not find." (Siduri to Gilgamesh, Tablet X, Foster 2001, as quoted by Robert Boyd Skipper, Substack)
critical_response: Widely adopted as a standard college text and used in the Norton Anthology of World Literature. Norton's publicity quotes praise for a 'scrupulous new translation' that conveys 'the archaic power and even something of the occasional humor' of the poem and, by collating the different ancient versions, makes available 'many vivid narrative episodes that will be new to most English readers.' The Biblical Review (2019, on the 2nd edition) calls it 'by far, the most accessible, accurate, and precise translation of the ancient text' but faults the edition for scattering artefact images without explaining that the iconography is not directly tied to the text. Scholarly surveys rate it as of a high standard alongside George (1999) [uncertain: specific journal reviews]
controversies: No accuracy dispute. The main scholarly caveat is methodological: harmonising Standard and Old Babylonian material into one narrative ('Gilgamesch-Harmonie') produces a story no ancient reader ever read, and silent restorations hide how uncertain some lines are. Foster defends both choices on grounds of audience. The 2019 edition dropped the Rivkah Harris essay on women in the epic and Hillary Major's poem, replacing them with essays by Susan Ackerman and Andrew George
regional_reception: An English-language classroom edition aimed at US college courses; no known Arabic or Kurdish edition and no recorded return to Iraq [uncertain]. Its reach is through the Norton anthologies and US survey courses rather than the region of origin
ai_craft_tension: Foster is a useful middle case between the philologist and the poet. The work a machine could plausibly assist with (reading signs, aligning Standard and Old Babylonian witnesses, proposing restorations) is exactly what Foster does as a scholar. But his decisive choices are editorial and aural: which centuries-apart fragments to sew together, which breaks are worth showing, and which lines sound 'lame' when read aloud. He openly rejects mechanical marking of every doubtful reading as 'a useless exercise in the typesetter's craft', a judgement about the reader's experience that no alignment model makes. The Norton frame also shows a human curation layer: choosing analogues and critical essays that tell students how to read the poem
essay_hooks: (1) Foster on his method: 'My rendering sews together material often centuries apart in time', a harmony no Babylonian ever read (World Literature Today, 2017). (2) 'Relentlessly marking minor problems with the manuscripts is largely a useless exercise in the typesetter's craft', a direct contrast with Kovacs's hundred-plus question marks. (3) His quality test was reading aloud: 'the lame lines came through with discouraging clarity.' (4) 'The pleasure and pain of translation is to try to play well on two difficult musical instruments at the same time.' (5) Tablet XII is cut from the epic and replaced by the older, fuller Sumerian poem in a separate section, a choice about what counts as the ending. (6) Gilgamesh's verdict after the snake: 'I have done a good deed for a reptile!' (7) Foster calls Andrew George's English translation 'by far the most authoritative in any language', a leading Assyriologist deferring to a rival version
